en: As the people stood thus,
Karacha, khan of the Noyguts,
Readied himself like a hawk.
He was one of the courageous men;
From the unseen, wisdom came to him.
“Your father's grave, wretched people!
When death arrives, must one not die?
What Allah lays upon one's head,
Must a poor mortal not endure?
Does the father not pursue, sweating?
Does the mother not give birth, weeping?
Does the mortal who is born not die?
To the decree rightly written,
Must the poor mortal not submit?
If He desires what He entrusted,
Will the Creator not take it Himself!”
Thus saying, Karacha,
His gilded side-pouch,
From above that side-pouch,
Now unfastened his white belt.
Grasping his life thin as a hair,
Readying himself to present Akkula,
Akkula, coming into his fifth year,
He had covered with costly cloth.
Karacha was a knowing man,
“Someone may do it harm,” he said,
And had it tended in a secluded place.
The gold-adorned halter
He had fastened with finery.
The white lead rope, round-braided,
He had attached, three armspans long.
“If only this were my horse,”
Able men admired it.
The white lead rope, round-braided,
He now folded and laid over its neck.
Toward the gray-maned warrior, Karacha
Now led Akkula as a gift.
Leading Akkula,
To present it to the bloodthirsty one,
Karacha walked bent low.
The many souls watching,
“Well, what will happen?” they said,
Unable to look, despairing of life.
When Karacha came close,
They walked away one by one;
All looked at the ground,
Their faces changing and paling,
Their voices reaching God.
If you looked at their heads,
They did not lift them, but buried them in the ground.
Unable to rise, they swayed,
Scratching the earth, trembling,
Muttering to one another.
The sensible grieved beyond measure;
The foolish then
Ran to the camel for shelter.
Walking slowly by the direct path,
Karacha brought the gift,
Making Kula step majestically,
Leading it to your mighty destroyer.
Turning his face toward the Truth,
Making Kula step majestically,
Karacha stood presenting it.
The coat Manas wore
Was mail with a golden collar.
Your champion touched by Kydyr,
Hanging his sword upon his wrist,
Awoke with a start,
Turned to his right,
Rose in wrath,
And implored the one God.
Faith shone upon his face.
Do not ask the gray-maned one's condition:
A true Muslim, a towering lion,
The fortress of these Kyrgyz,
A mighty warrior to protect them.
When Manas rose and looked,
Akkula had come as a gift,
With a long tail and a mane,
Such a beautiful creature!
Looking, his heart was drawn to it.
At that very moment Akkula
Seemed nearer than his father.
Girding his waist firmly,
Raising the cry ‘The faith of Islam!’
Raiding Beijing and attacking,
It was a horse to ride through hardship.
Enduring firmly over forty mountain passes,
It was a horse to ride into combat.
Between unbelievers and Muslims,
Stepping majestically,
It was a horse to ride into battle.
Grasping a spear, breaking the ranks,
It was a horse to ride into uproar.
Battle cries deafening ears,
It was a horse to ride into tumult.
Taking a red-tasseled spear,
Girding on a sword without a sheath,
It was a horse to ride into slaughter.
Taking a black-tasseled spear,
Girding on a black-steel sword,
It was a horse to ride into combat.
Between unbelievers and Muslims,
Dividing the frontier,
It was a horse to ride into battle.
Leading ninety vast hosts,
It was a horse to ride on a raid.
Leading eighty vast hosts,
It was a horse to ride into the clash.
Taking a tasseled spear in hand,
Trotting with a swaying stride,
Coming out alone to joust,
It was the one to brighten a face;
It was a horse to ride on patrol.
What the saint Babadyikan
Had said was this very thing.
My Allah Most High had brought
Akkula himself.
Manas rejoiced, swelling with pride,
His nose flaring like a leather flask.
Rising like a gray lion,
Imploring the Creator,
Your bloodthirsty one, vast as a mountain,
Rose from his place in readiness.
When Manas stood up,
His heart was drawn to the horse.
The great dun being led
Appeared like the horse Buraq.
“Yesterday, aged Babadyikan's
Words have surely come true.
The dun horse he spoke of,
This is the very one.
Broad chest, low mane,
Hoe-like hooves, broad croup,
Wild-sheep legs, a spring-trap back:
It is a horse to endure long distances.
Its sire is a spirit-steed of the mountains,
Its dam a courser of the desert.
Bringing it perfectly, making it perfectly,
God has ordained this.
Loading eighty camels with gold coins,
If one traveled the face of the earth,
Scattering and spending gold,
Never would one meet its like.
The four corners of the round world,
If one searched four times around,
A lord would not find its like.
Encountered from the unseen,
The Creator had made it;
My dear Akkula
Was found from a stranger.
Short forelock and mane,
Ah, dear Akkula,
It is a horse to dispel misfortune!
It is no ordinary tail and mane,
No horse to take for nothing!
This old man bringing the horse,
This mighty khan of sacred power,
To the Noygut Kyrgyz themselves
Has become a father.
The dear Muslim,
‘Let magnanimous Manas ride it,’ he said,
And has brought it here!
Let me heed his request;
Red wheat and much property,
Let me give as a gift for Kula.
If he is not content with wheat,
Let me heed his request;
Wealthy Jakyp's countless cattle,
Let me give them all as a gift.
Spending all my wealth,
Let me accept his words.
My living soul,
Everything in my hands,
Let me offer for one horse.
One hoof is worth countless cattle.
To the servant He does not wish to favor,
It will not come for a purchase price;
He sets it ready upon the path
Of the servant He wishes to favor.
If it chases wild asses, none escape;
It has a whirlwind's swiftness.
Ridden on scouting, it will not tire;
My dear Akkula
Has Duldul's prowess.
Its horsehair tail is an armful;
The Maker favored me and brought it.
Majestically stepping Akkula
Was found for my good fortune!”
Before he had closed his mouth after speaking,
Your magnanimous one now stood up.
His white turban like a cauldron,
Karacha, khan of the Noyguts,
His shouting voice like the call to prayer,
The great dun horse he led,
He presented, standing tall.
Both hands against his breast,
He turned his face toward the Truth.
At the edge of the white wheat,
Akkula, swift among horses,
Making its dark form gleam,
He stood presenting it.
Karacha stood and said:
“Oh, my son, you appear different;
When I look, my heart is drawn to you.
A company of nine supports you;
You have the marks of greatness.
Among spearmen, exceedingly
You have the marks of skill.
To become master of the people,
You have the marks of greatness.
To bring the people into your hands,
You have the marks of one who can take them.
To those who challenge you, devastation—
You have the marks of one who can bring it.
Broad-chested, wise man,
(Of places heard of and seen,
How many lands have I traveled!)
I have never seen a lion mighty as you!
Your very scalp appears different.
‘If my son were like this,’ I say;
When I look, my heart is drawn to you.
Beside you is wheat like a mountain.
Praying to the Creator,
I am asking who you are.
Created upon the face of the earth,
There are seventy kinds of people.
Tell me plainly, my foal:
Who are your father's kin?
Whose name is your battle cry, who are your people?
Who are your kin, what is your lineage?
Who are your forefathers, your village?
Tell me, my foal,
Who are you in your deepest origins?
If you do not take offense,
Where is the land where your village camps?
Your forefathers' battle cry—
I ask who you are; who are your people?
Please do not grow angry.
I came humbly to you;
Do not slaughter me before my appointed death!
I have begun a conversation;
I am a white-bearded old man.
I asked your father's lineage;
To hear who you are,
I am filled with longing!
When I look from either side,
Your form appears blessed by Kydyr.
When I look at your forehead,
Your form appears kingly.
Curse this mortal frailty:
Unable to withstand your face's fury,
I stand in fear.
When I look from your right,
A black-spotted leopard
Charges from your flank.
